Question: A 14 yr old suffers traumatic avulsion of 11 and 21 while playing hockey and immediately puts them back in sockets. He came to your clinic 15 mins later. The treatment is?
Option A: Remove from the socket and reimplant with splint
Explanation:
The ideal way to transport the tooth is to have it replaced in its socket, even though it needs to be repositioned in the dentist’s office. If an avulsed tooth can be replanted at the site of injury, the prognosis is better than waiting until the patient is transported to a treatment facility.

The following advice can be given over the telephone to someone able to assist the victim:
• Rinse the tooth in cold running water.
• Do not scrub the tooth.
• Replace the tooth in the socket.
• Bring the patient to the dental office right away to complete the treatment of replantation.

Note: Antibiotics should be administered after replantation. Coverage is for 5 to 7 days.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Identify what is shown in IOPA
Explanation:
Classification of posts based on material:
Posts can be made from non-metallic materials and metals.

Non-Metallic:
• These posts show a lower incidence of root fracture due to their ability to resist high stress without permanent deformation and breaking.
• They should not be used if there is insufficient sound tooth tissue. The sound tooth tissue should be at least 1.5mm circumferentially further apical to the core.
• Also, more aesthetic than metal posts as their optical properties are closer to tooth tissue (except for carbon fibre posts due to the darker material).
• Non-metallic posts are easier to remove from teeth if needed than metal posts. Prefabricated non-metallic posts are most common in use but they can also be built up in the laboratory.

Zirconia: Zirconia posts have high strength. However, they are brittle and have a high modulus which can potentially lead to root fracture. It can be difficult to remove the posts if needed.

Ceramic: Ceramic posts are made from a brittle material. These posts can be too strong which can lead to root fracture. It can be difficult and even impossible to remove a ceramic post.

Fibre reinforced resins (FRC): Fibre reinforced resins are a form of non-metallic posts and include carbon fibre, fiberglass and woven polyethylene ribbon-reinforced composites. These posts are more likely to fail as their fibres can fray.

Carbon fibre: Carbon fibre posts show very little deformation and can absorb and transfer forces similarly to dentine. However, these posts can be dark in colour which may lead to an unaesthetic result as the post can shine through the tooth.

Glass fibre/Fibre glass: Glass fibre Posts are less brittle than ceramic posts. Posts that have unidirectional fibres are the strongest. However, it is difficult to produce this type of material as fibre bundles require infiltration and wetting with resin. This process can often leave voids on the surface of the fibres, leading to a weakened structure.

Metallic: Traditionally metal posts have been used due to the good corrosion resistance and high yield strength. They look more radiopaque. Some are serrated or threaded (prefabricated) and some are smooth (custom made cast metal) posts.

Prefabricated metal posts
• Stainless steel, titanium, titanium alloy and gold alloy are used to construct prefabricated posts.
• These types of posts are usually placed in the post space and the core is constructed with a direct restorative core material.
• There are also prefabricated posts for which cores are cast onto. These posts are usually made of Type IV gold alloy (containing gold, platinum, palladium and iridium) or platinum, gold and iridium alloys, which are compatible with palladium and silver-free alloys or platinum, gold, palladium and silver alloy.

Cast metal posts
Often a metal alloy such as Type IV gold alloy is used.

Radiographic appearance of posts:
• High radiopacity of a post makes radiographic visualization and verification easier and may reduce unwarranted retreatment of teeth.
• Earlier the aesthetic posts had radiopacity similar to that of dentin. Now they are available in a range of radiopacities.
• Metallic posts are highly radiopaque. Threaded posts will cast their threads in the radiograph.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: IOPA image of 11-year-old with injury to Central incisor and pulp exposure reported to a dentist. What will be the ideal treatment plan?
Explanation:
The age of the boy is 11 years, that means root maturation is still in process. The radiograph also shows the evidence of immature root apex and thin root canal walls. The boy immediately reported to the clinic, so the best treatment is doing an apexogenesis procedure.

Apexogenesis:
Refers to a vital pulp therapy procedure performed to encourage physiological development and formation of the root end.

Rationale:
• Maintenance of the integrity of the radicular pulp tissue to allow continued root growth.
• Root end development occurs in a tooth with a normal pulp and minimal inflammation.
• Pulp of immature teeth has significant reparative potential.
• Pulp revascularisation and repair occurs more efficiently in tooth with an open apex.
• Relatively thin dentin of immature roots and open apex are prone to fracture when attempted to do normal root canal treatment.

Goals:
• Sustaining a viable Hertwig’s sheath to allow continued development of root length for a favorable crown: root ratio.
• Maintaining pulp vitality to help maturation of root.
• Promoting root-end closure to create a natural apical constriction.
• Generating a dentinal bridge at the site of pupotomy. (a sign that the pulp has maintained its vitality).

Indications:
• Indicated for traumatized or pulpally involved vital permanent tooth when root apex is incompletely formed.
• No history of spontaneous pain.
• No sensitivity on percussion.
• No Hemorrhage.
• No periapical radiolucency.
• Traumatic Luxation.

Contraindications:
• Evidence that radicular pulp has undergone degenerative changes.
• Tooth with unfavourable horizontal root fracture i.e. close to gingival margin.
• Purulent drainage.
• History of prolonged pain.
• Necrotic debris in canal.
• Periapical Radiolucency.

Question: In a 12-year-old female child, there was avulsion of a tooth which was reimplanted by a nearby dentist within 60 mins, the child has been taken to another dentist after one week, what should be done
Option A: Maintain oral hygiene and observe for 3 months.
Option B: Remove splint immediately and no other treatment is required.
Option C: Plan immediate RCT and remove splint
Option D: Splint retained for 4 weeks followed by RCT
Explanation:
12-year child means we should assume the root is complete. If this is the case, after one week ideally the splint treatment should be started.

Protocol for endodontic treatment in different cases of avulsion:

1. Extra oral dry time < 60 min
• Closed apex- start RCT in the second week
• Open apex- avoid endodontic treatment and look for signs of revascularization. If pulp becomes infected, initiate apexification in the later week.

2. Extra oral dry time > 60 min
• Closed apex- start RCT in the second week
• Open apex- in this case the endodontic treatment should be preferably done outside the mouth before replantation. If endodontic treatment was not done before replantation, initiate apexification in the later week.

After the tooth is replanted in 60 minutes, stabilized with a splint. The splint should be removed, antibiotics are discontinued, and endodontic treatment should be preferably done outside the mouth before replantation if possible. If endodontic treatment was not done before replantation, initiate endodontic treatment and look for signs of revascularization.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: DPC is indicated for tooth and the dentist plan for re-visit, what will be the material used
Explanation:
(Ca(OH)2 has been the material of choice for pulp capping but it has several disadvantages like, unsatisfactory adherence to dentin, dissolution over time, and multiple tunnel defects in the dentin bridges.

Mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) is recommended as an alternative for Ca(OH)2 as the stimulation of dentin-bridge formation is faster allowing pulp healing and showed high success rates in clinical procedures. MTA is a bioactive, biocompatible, antibacterial material with good stability, and excellent sealing ability. However, its long setting time, poor handling properties, high material cost, and the discoloration potential remain a challenge to the practitioner. Slower setting and discoloration of dental tissues occurs.

Direct pulp capping can be done in one or two visits. In one visit DPC, the cavity will not be re-entered again. The most common materials used for one visit are Dycal (calcium hydroxide fast set), Biodentin.

The prolonged setting time of MTA happens to be a clinical weakness that may prevent its routine use as a DPC agent in single visit restoration of deeply carious teeth. MTA has been shown to be a reliable direct pulp capping (DPC) material on carious exposures in permanent teeth when two-visit treatment protocol was observed. As MTA setting time is long and needs moisture for setting, a moist cotton pellet will be placed over MTA capping material and temporary restoration will be placed.

After 24 hrs, the revisit should be planned, and a final restoration should be planned. Or else after a delay of 45 min, the final restoration can be given in the same visit.

In the present question since the dentist planned a revisit suggests that he used MTA for DPC. Formocresol is not very suitable as DPC agent.

Question: C-shaped canals are present in?
Option B: Mand. incisor> Mand. 1st molar > Mand. 3rd molar
Explanation:
C shaped canals are seen in teeth which has higher incidence of root fusion. C shaped canals are formed from the fusion of the mesial and distal roots on either the buccal or the lingual root surfaces. The order of C-shaped canals are:
Mandibular second molar > mandibular first molar > mandibular 3rd molar > maxillary 2nd molar > maxillary 3rd molar > mandibular premolar > lateral incisor.

Question: Which of the following methods is used to sterilize guttapercha:
Explanation: Gutta-percha points, due to their chemical and physical properties are not amenable to the usual methods of physical sterilization in an autoclave or hot air oven. Therefore, chemical sterilization is mandatory for effective sterilization of gutta-percha points. Sequeira et al studied the effectiveness of 4 chemical solutions in eliminating B. subtilis spores on gutta-percha cones. The solutions tested were 5.25% Sodium hypochlorite, 2% Glutaraldehyde, 2% Chlorhexidine gluconate and 70% Ethyl alcohol. The results showed that 5.25% Sodium hypochlorite was effective in destroying the spores after one minute of immersion time. Among the options provided ethyl alcohol is the best pick.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Property exhibited by NiTi wires is?
Explanation: Pseudoelasticity, sometimes called superelasticity, is an elastic (reversible) response to an applied stress, caused by a phase transformation between the austenitic and martensitic phases of a crystal. It is exhibited in shape-memory alloys like Ni-Ti. Superelastic alloys belong to the larger family of shape-memory alloys. When mechanically loaded, a superelastic alloy deforms reversibly to very high strains (up to 10%) by the creation of a stress-induced phase. When the load is removed, the new phase becomes unstable and the material regains its original shape.

Question: All are true regarding post and core except
Option A: posts should be placed in the primary roots (palatal root of Max. molars and distal roots of Mand. molars)
Option B: should not be extended more than 7 mm apical to the origin of the root canal in the base of the pulp chamber.
Option C: Each millimeter of increase (beyond one-third the root diameter) causes a eight fold increase in the potential for root fracture
Option D: Optimal post diameter measurements have been determined to be about 0.6 mm for Mand. incisors
Explanation:
Post length:
• Since 5 mm of gutta-percha should be retained apically to ensure a good seal (as measured radiographically), posts should be extended to that length in all teeth except molars. With molars, posts should be placed in the primary roots (palatal root of maxillary molars and distal roots of mandibular molars)
• Should not be extended more than 7 mm apical to the origin of the root canal in the base of the pulp chamber. Extension beyond this length can lead to root perforation or only very thin areas of remaining tooth structure.

Post diameter:
• A frequently used and clinically appropriate guideline for post diameter is to not exceed one-third the root diameter. It has been determined that when a root canal is prepared for a post and the diameter is increased beyond one-third of the root diameter, the tooth becomes exponentially weaker. Each millimeter of increase (beyond one-third the root diameter) causes a six-fold increase in the potential for root fracture.

Based on measuring the root dimensions of 1,500 teeth (125 of each tooth) and using the guideline that the post should be one-third the root diameter, optimal post diameter measurements have been determined to be about 0.6 mm for mandibular incisors and 1.0 mm for maxillary central incisors, maxillary and mandibular canines, and the palatal root of the maxillary first molar. The recommended post diameter for the other teeth was 0.8 mm.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: All are reasonably true of post-preparation except:
Option A: Should go at least 4 mm apical to alveolar crest for minimization of dentin stresses
Option B: In an average rooted tooth, should go inside the canal by one-third the root length
Option C: Should go up to 7 mm in molar roots, from the Cvek chamber floor
Option D: In average-length roots, the post should be prepared so that a 5 mm apical plug of gutta-percha is left
Explanation:
Option ‘A’ is True: Going at least 4 mm apical to the alveolar crest helps minimize stress concentrations and provides sufficient post length for retention.

Option 'B' is incorrect: The length of the post inside the canal must be equal to or greater than that of the crown, or two-thirds the length of the root to achieve maximum retention.

Option 'C' is True: In molars, particularly when using Cvek technique, the post should go not more than 7 mm apical to the pulpal floor to avoid perforation or thinning of the root.

Option 'D' is True: A minimum of 4-5 mm of gutta-percha must be preserved apically to maintain an adequate seal and prevent failure of the root canal treatment.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Which is true regarding post-space preparation?
Option B: Increased diameter increases retention and is recommended
Option C: Preparation depth should be minimized due to root concavities
Explanation:
Peeso reamer is used mostly for post space preparation. End cutting bur not used. Option ‘A’ is false.

Post diameter should not exceed one-third the root canal diameter. Each millimeter of increase (beyond one-third the root diameter) causes a six-fold increase in the potential for root fracture. Option 'B' false.

The most appropriate roots for post preparation are the palatal roots in maxillary molars and are the distal roots of mandibular molars. The facial roots of maxillary molars and the mesial root of mandibular molars should be avoided, if at all possible, due to their concavities. If these roots must be used in addition to the primary roots, then the post length should be short (3 to 4 mm) and a small-diameter instrument should be used. Option 'C' is true.

Explanation: Gutta-percha endodontic filling points contain approximately 20% gutta-percha (matrix), 65% zinc oxide (filler), 10% heavy metal sulfates (radiopacifier), and 5% waxes and/or resins (plasticizer). Explanation:

Question: 8-year-old presented with complicated crown Nolla’s 7, few days after injury, pulp response negative, the treatment is?
Explanation:
The following interceptions can be derived in the present case:
• 8 yr old Nolla’s 7- the root apex is not completely formed.

• Nolla‘s stages of tooth calcification:
0 - absence of crypts; 1 - presence of crypts; 2 - initial calcification; 3 - 1/3 of crown completed; 4-2/3 of crown completed; 5-crown almost completed; 6 - crown completed; 7 - 1/3 of root completed; 8 - 2/3 of root completed; 9 - root almost completed—open apex; 10 - apical end of root completed.

• Complicated crown fracture- that means the pulp is involved.
• Pulp responded negative

Since only 1/3 root is completed, there will be thin dentinal walls which may fracture if RCT is attempted. So RCT is excluded. Apexification and revascularization are the options left out. Among these, revascularization seems to be more appropriate.

Revascularization:
This is a new treatment method for immature (open apex) necrotic permanent teeth. This technique allows the growth of root even when the pulp is necrotic. This helps in strengthening and avoiding damage to the remaining thin and fragile walls of the immature tooth. The aim of this technique is stimulating the residual apical pulp stem cells which can survive due to the abundant blood supply in the open apex cases.

Revascularization procedure aids in:
• Stimulation of odontoblasts or undifferentiated mesenchymal cells at the periapex.
• Deposition of the calcific material at the apex as well as lateral dentinal walls.
• Normal maturation of the entire root.

Question: Helical angle:
Option A: Angle between leading edge and long axis
Option B: Angle between first and second cutting thread
Option C: Angle between tip of instrument with long axis
Option D: Angle between first thread with long axis
Explanation:
Helix or helical angle - Helix angle is an angle between the cutting edge (leading edge) and the long axis of a file. Helix angle plays an important role in debris collection and it also determines the direction of rotation. Helix angle can be constant or variable (changes along the length of a file). Variable helix angles decrease the screw in effect when most of the working surface of a file is engaged and it can decrease the torsion stress on a file.

Design features of rotary instruments in endodontics:
1. Taper is described as the amount of file diameter increase per millimeter along the working surface from the tip toward the file handle. ISO files have 2% taper, but rotary files range from 2-12% taper. Some of the newer instruments have a variable taper built into the instrument. Thus, within a single instrument the taper varies. Eg: Protaper
2. Flutes are the grooves on the working side of the files which can be produced either by twisting or grinding a wire. Flutes provide cutting edges and also space for debris collection. Therefore, their presence turns a wire into a shaping instrument which both cuts the tooth structure and acts as an auger. The depth, width, number, arrangement and the direction of the flutes play an important role on the behavior of a file.
3. Helix or helical angle - Helix angle is an angle between the cutting edge (leading edge) and the long axis of a file. Helix angle plays an important role in debris collection and it also determines the direction of rotation. Helix angle can be constant or variable (changes along the length of a file). Variable helix angles decrease the screw in effect when most of the working surface of a file is engaged and it can decrease the torsion stress on a file.
4. Radial land - The radial land is the peripheral portion of a rotary instrument that is flat and smooth designed to center the instrument in the central space.

Explanation: The goal of resected root end is to create optimum conditions for the growth of cementum and subsequent regeneration of the periodontal ligament across the resected root end. Subject: Endodontics
Question: STEM cells most commonly harvested from:
Option B: Stem cells from Human Exfoliated Deciduous teeth
Explanation:
Cells which have a remarkable capacity for self-renewal and potency and can give rise to different types of cells and tissues are called stem cells.

Dental stem cells isolated from different parts of the teeth are:
1. Stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SHED)
2. Adult dental pulp stem cells (DPSC)
3. Stem cells from the apical part of the papilla (SCAP)
4. Stem cells from the dental follicle (DFSC)
5. Periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSC)
6. Bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSC)

Dental stem cells can be isolated from pulp, which harbors neural crest differentiated stem cells. Dental pulp is easily accessible tissue which has less morbidity after harvesting. They can be harvested from both deciduous teeth (stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth [SHED]) and adult teeth (teeth removed for orthodontic purposes, impacted teeth, and supernumerary teeth).

Dental pulp is a remarkable site of stem cells for the following reasons:
• Collecting stem cells from dental pulp is a non-invasive practice that can be performed in the adult during life and in the young after surgical extraction of wisdom teeth, a common surgical practice.
• Tissue sacrifice is very low when collecting dental pulp stem cells. Several cytotypes can be obtained from dental pulp stem cells owing to their multipotency; transplantation of new-formed bone tissue obtained from dental pulp stem cells leads to the formation of vascularized adult bone and integration between the graft and the surrounding host blood supply.
• Dental pulp stem cells can be cryopreserved and stored for long periods; dental pulp is ideal for tissue engineering; for clinical use in several pathologies requiring bone tissue growth.
• Thus the dental pulp is a remarkable site of stem cells and collecting stem cells from dental pulp is a non-invasive practice that can be performed in the adult during life and in the young after surgical extraction of wisdom teeth, a common surgical practice.

Tooth selection for dental stem cell banking should satisfy the requirements given below:
a) Deciduous teeth
• Pulp should appear red in color indicating blood supply
• Deciduous teeth with two third of root are preferred
• Posterior deciduous teeth are not preferred because of less pulp and chance of infection due to longer retention in the mouth than anterior
• Extracted teeth are preferred than exfoliated teeth.

b) Adult teeth
• Only vital teeth should be harvested
• Teeth with infection and any pathology is not preferred
• Periodontally compromised teeth cannot be harvested
• Teeth should have a sufficient amount of pulp.

Explanation:

Subject: Endodontics
Question: MTA-D and tetraclean differ in
Option B: conc. of antibiotic and % of acid
Explanation:
Recently, MTA-D and Tetraclean, two new irrigants based on a mixture of antibiotics, citric acid, and a detergent, have been developed.

• MTA-D is the first irrigating solution created which is capable of removing both the smear layer and disinfecting the root canal system. It is a mixture of 3% doxycycline hyclate, 4.25% citric acid, and 0.5% polysorbate-80 (Tween 80) detergent. MTA-D has been recommended in clinical practice as a final rinse after completion of conventional chemo-mechanical preparation.
• Tetraclean is another combination product similar to MTA-D. The two irrigants differ in the concentration of antibiotics (doxycycline 150 mg/5 ml for MTA-D and 50 mg/5 ml for Tetraclean) and the kind of detergent (Tween 80 for MTA-D, polypropylene glycol for Tetraclean).

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Patient come with an avulsed tooth within 60 min of trauma; the treatment protocol involves
Explanation:
After avulsion, preparation of root:

A) Extra oral dry time is less than 60 minutes
i) Closed apex
The root should be rinsed of debris with water or saline, replanted in as gentle as possible.

ii) Open apex
The tooth is soaked in doxycycline or covered with minocycline for 5 minutes, debris is gently rinsed off and the tooth is replanted.

B) Extraoral dry time more than 60 minutes
i) Closed apex
The periodontal ligament is removed by placing it in 3% citric acid for 3 minutes, soaking it in fluoride or covering the root with emdogain (A enamel matrix derivative that stimulates the regeneration of periodontal ligament) and then replanting.

ii) Open apex
If replantation is to take place, the open apex is treated the same as the closed apex tooth. Endodontic treatment may be performed out of the mouth.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Corrosion of NiTi instruments occur if immersed in warm NaOCl for more than
Explanation:
Corrosion of NiTi instruments occur in the clinical setting when the instruments are immersed in warmed NaOCl for longer than 60 minutes. Surface irregularities may also provide access to corrosive substances, most notably sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl).

• Some studies have suggested that chloride corrosion may lead to micropitting and possibly subsequent fracture in NiTi instruments.
• Not only immersion in various disinfecting solutions for extended periods (e.g., overnight) produced corrosion of NiTi instruments and subsequent decreased torsional resistance, but for ProTaper, RaCe, and ProFile instruments, also short-term immersion.
• Regular cleaning and sterilization procedures do not seem to affect NiTi rotary instruments.
• In one study, only limited material loss occurred when NiTi Light-Speed instruments were immersed in 1% and 5% NaOCl for 30 to 60 minutes.
• Although sterilization procedures per se do not have an impact on NiTi integrity, there is an ongoing discussion over the impact of other aspects of clinical usage on the mechanical properties of NiTi rotaries.

Question: On a tooth after bleaching, the minimum time gap required to place composite resin restoration without affecting its’ strength is
Explanation:
Many studies suggest that a time interval of at least 7 days should be allowed between enamel bleaching and placement of adhesive bonding agents for accomplishment of composite resin restorations. It is very critical that immediate bonding of resin after bleaching will alter and compromise bond strength of composite to bleached tooth structure. This reduction in bond strength after bleaching is time dependent. The delaying of bonding procedure after bleaching should be performed after at least seven days following in office bleaching.

For best results composite resin placement should be delayed for 2 weeks after bleaching, to allow for dissipation of residual peroxides that would interfere with the bonding agent.

Rule of thumb wait for 3 weeks after completion of home-bleaching before placing composite- Restorative dentistry by Italian Academy of restorative and home-bleaching before placing composite- Restorative dentistry.

Question: Mid-treatment emergencies in endodontics are seen maximum in
Explanation:
The Endo emergencies can be classified as:
1. Pretreatment emergencies
2. Interappointment emergencies
3. Post-endodontic emergencies

Pretreatment:
• Pulpal pain
• Reversible pulpitis
• Irreversible pulpitis
• Acute periapical abscess
• Cracked tooth syndrome

During treatment (Interappointment):
• Recent restorative treatment
• Periodontal treatment
• Exposure of the pulp
• Fracture of the root or crown
• Pain as a result of instrumentation
• acute apical periodontitis
• Phoenix abscess

Post-endodontic treatment:
• High restoration
• Overfilling
• Root end filling
• Root fracture

Flare Up
• Described as the occurrence of pain, swelling or the combination of these during the course of root canal therapy, which results in unscheduled visits by patients.

• Contributing factors for flareup:
- Age: patients in the 40-59 yrs range have the most flareups
- Gender: females more than males
- Systemic conditions: allergies to various substance
- Tooth type: mandibular more than maxillary teeth
- Presence of preoperative pain/swelling: patients who take analgesics and anti-inflammatories to prevent preoperative pain more incidence of flareups.
- Number of visits: multivisit RCT more flareups than single visit
- Pulpal/periapical status: Teeth with necrotic pulps more prone to mid endodontic flare-ups than vital teeth. Teeth with periapical lesion more than without periapical lesion.

Question: Tooth is sensitive to hot and relieved by cold is most likely suffering from
Explanation:
Pulp necrosis:

A necrotic pulp should be suspected when the tooth does not respond to pulp sensibility tests. Occasionally, patients will complain of a dull continuous ache that is exacerbated by heat but relieved by cold water being held over the tooth. The reason is unknown although it has been speculated that micro-organisms producing gases may infect the necrotic pulp and these gases contract with application of the cold water which relieves pressure on the nerve endings that may still be vital in the apical portion of the pulp. However, the relief from the cold cath is temporary and the pain returns as the tooth warms up again and the gases expand. This phenomenon occurs since the apical part of the pulp is the last part of the pulp to necrose. It is possible that the apical nerves maintain some vascular supply to their more medial portions for a short time after the rest of the pulp has died.

In advanced stages of irreversible pulpitis of teeth, there might be partial necrosis of pulp with pulpal inflammation giving mixed responses; also pain may be exacerbated by heat but relieved by cold water.

Question: Blood supply to pulp
Explanation:
Capillaries function as exchange vessels regulating the transport of diffusion of substances between blood and local interstitial tissue elements. They consist of single layer of endothelium surrounded by basement membrane.

Based on the property of semi permeability capillaries may be grouped as:

Class I: Fenestrated capillaries
These structures are characterized by endothelium with openings (fenestrations) in the capillary walls. These fenestrations can be open or occluded by a thin diaphragm. Fenestrated capillaries are found in dense networks in dental pulp as well as in the renal glomerulus, the intestinal mucosa, and the sulcular gingiva.

Class II: Continuous capillaries (non-fenestrated)
These vascular structures are defined by endothelium devoid of fenestrations. Continuous capillaries are found in dental pulp as well as in heart, lung, and muscle.

Class III: Discontinuous capillaries
These capillaries consist of discontinuous endothelium with wide intercellular spaces of approximately 5 to 10 nm. The basement membrane is also discontinuous. Discontinuous endothelium is found in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow.

Class IV: Tight junction Capillaries
found in the central nervous system and the retina.

NOTE : Class I & II capillaries are present in the dental pulp.

The microcirculatory Organization of the subodontoblastic region is divided into three major layers. The terminal capillary network is located in the first layer, also called the odontoblastic layer. The second layer, also known as the capillary network, contains precapillary and postcapillary vessels organized adjacent to the odontoblastic layer. The third layer consists of a venular network of vessels. During aging, there is a general reduction in pulpal metabolism, and the capillary organization is often simplified and becomes one single layer of capillaries terminating directly into venules.

Question: Best method to diagnose non-odontogenic pain:
Option D: Case history recording, step by step testing and evaluation of cause
Explanation:
Clinical Characteristics of Odontogenic Pain:
• Mainly inflammatory
• An identifiable condition that reasonably explains the symptoms
• Response to local noxious stimulation is proportionate and predictable
• Local anesthesia of the suspected tooth eliminates the pain
• During chewing, the tooth feels sore or elongated. Discomfort is often felt when biting pressure is released rather than while it is sustained.

TypeClinical characteristics
Myofascial toothache• Pain is non-pulsatile
• Not responsive to local provocation of the tooth
• Pain increases with function of involved muscle (Trigger points)
• Local anesthetic of the tooth does not affect the toothache
• Local anesthetic of the involved muscle (trigger point) reduces the toothache
Neurovascular Toothache• Pain has periods of remission. Episodes of pain may pose a temporal behavior appearing at similar times during the day, week or month
• Lack of reasonable dental cause of pain
• May follow after headache, sinusitis, dental treatment, surgery or trauma, appearing complication of a former experience
Cardiac Toothache• Presence of aching pain that is cyclic
• Toothache is increased with physical exertion or exercise
• Toothache is associated with chest pains
• Toothache is decreased with nitroglycerin tablets
• Local anesthetic does not arrest the toothache
• Cardiac pain characterized by heaviness, throbbing pain in substernal region which radiate to left shoulder, arm, neck, and mandible
Neuropathic Toothache/neuralgia• Unilateral, sudden, sharp, severe, lacerating and shock-like (paroxysmal)
• Provoked by relatively innocuous peripheral stimulation of a “trigger zone” or may occur spontaneously
• Local anesthetic at the tooth will not reduce the pain unless it also represents the “trigger zone” (very rare)
• Local anesthetic at the “trigger zone” will reduce the attacks
• Patient is typically asymptomatic between the episodes
Sinus Toothache• Patient reports pressure or pain below the eyes
• Toothache is increased with lowering of the head
• Toothache is increased with applied pressure over the involved sinus
• Local anesthetic of the tooth does not eliminate the pain
• Diagnosis can be confirmed by air/fluid level seen in appropriate imaging
Psychogenic Toothache• Patient reports that multiple teeth are often painful with frequent change in character and location
• Patient presents with chronic pain behavior
• Lack of response to reasonable dental treatment
• Unusual or unexpected response to therapy
• No other identifiable pain condition that can explain the toothache

So proper case history recording, step by step testing and evaluation of cause will help to differentiate non odontogenic pains.
